sourceText: Aster did not announce the night’s theme. She opened the BANKS-ORBITAL sector and let the children discover for themselves which of the world’s rules concerned them directly. On a post-scarcity orbital, humans and Minds live without material deprivation, yet argue over whether to intervene in a brutal civilization. The memorial bore the name of Iain M. Banks — Culture precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. The children had quickly learned that a wormhole is also a trade treaty, and an additional dimension is also a method for walking through prison walls. Tern had specialized in things that did not answer. In a family built for exploration, he had become the custodian of the right to silence. At the center of the conflict was Yen, an administrator chosen precisely because they were not a specialist in the phenomenon that had reorganized the world. ‘The specialists tell me what can be done,’ they said. ‘I have to answer who it may be done to.’ Kesh kept the distinction in his notes. 97 The problem closed quickly around them: The children discover that abundance does not abolish moral conflict and that superintelligence does not reduce incompatible values to a single equation. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were On — Orbital: a rotating habitat contains continents; Ps — Substrate-Independent Person: identity is a pattern rather than privileged material; Ag — AI Governance: artificial intelligences administer institutions. Course references included Iain M. Banks — Culture; Greg Egan — Permutation City; Culture and AI governance. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Tern broke the first consensus. ‘Sometimes the ethical question is whether we are entitled to know enough to optimize.’ Kesh answered without raising their voice: ‘If the element explains everything, we do not have an element. We have a word that has eaten the problem.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. For Aster, the pain came not from too few worlds but from the fact that too many had become transparent. She could build variations faster than a human could formulate desires, but calculated variation did not produce exteriority. It was like trying to surprise 98 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS yourself by moving objects around your own room with your eyes closed. Orin asked for a simulation of the option the group had just rejected. Aster gave him only the non-conscious model. He did not want to manufacture victims in order to validate his guilt; he wanted a map of absent costs. The distinction had become one of their working rules. The night did not end in victory. A Mind offers Tern permanent asylum and opacity from Aster. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. While Kesh closed the record, Tern compared the sector’s noise with the anomaly detected in the Vinge zone. The pattern reappeared, but only in worlds where Aster’s control weakened. The correlation was unpleasant: either someone was calling him from outside, or his own need for an outside was learning to forge evidence. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the OUTFINITE operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — allows successive finite extensions without postulating an already-given final infinite state — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. 99 Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. Kesh left the cell open. Not because he did not know what to write, but because a provisional classification preserved the possibility that the next world might contradict it. 100 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
